SK3510 A variable already owned by using is disposed again

Dispose() is called by hand on a variable whose using disposes it at the end of the scope anyway.

CategoryLifetime
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since1.3

Why

A using disposes its resource when the scope ends, on every path including the exceptional one, so an explicit Dispose() on the same variable is a second call that the language guarantees will happen. Double disposal is only harmless for a type whose Dispose is idempotent — the framework asks for that and not every type delivers it, and a second call that releases a handle number the process has since reissued corrupts an unrelated file rather than throwing. Deleting the call removes the second disposal without changing when the first one happens.

Example

Instead of:

void Copy(string path) {
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    Read(stream);
    stream.Dispose();
}

Write:

void Copy(string path) {
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    Read(stream);
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The fix is safe because of a language guarantee rather than an analysis. A using variable is read-only, so nothing between the declaration and the explicit call can have made the two disposals land on different objects; the rule does not have to prove it. ⚠ Ownership is read from the variable's own declarator, never from an enclosing using that happens to name the same identifier — a shadowing local of the same name in an inner scope is a different symbol and is not reported. ⚠ The call must be an entire statement directly inside a block: if (failed) reader.Dispose(); is the same redundancy and is not reported, because deleting the statement would leave an if with no body, and a fix that produces text which does not parse is the one failure a fixing tool may not have. A Dispose() whose result is read, or one behind an &&, has nothing the fix can remove. ⚠ The invoked member is resolved by the semantic model and must be the parameterless disposal contract the using will itself invoke — Dispose is an ordinary identifier and a type may declare one that does something else. Close() is not reported: it is a different method, it is not always an alias for Dispose, and deleting it is not the same edit. A call reached across a lambda or a local function is skipped, because when that body runs is not something the enclosing using says anything about.
